Three things worth fixing in memory, because they are the usual slips:

Poisson and exponential are the same process seen two ways. If events arrive at
constant rate \lambda, the count in a fixed window is Poisson and the gap between
consecutive events is exponential. “Number of X per Y” is a count; “time until the next X”
is a waiting time.

A binomial count requires the number of trials n to be fixed before you start. If the
number of trials is itself the random thing you are counting, the count is not binomial.

\mathcal{N} takes the variance, not the standard deviation, throughout this book —
\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2). Misreading \sigma^2 = 4 as \sigma = 4 is the single most
common error with this notation.

Geometric convention. The form above counts trials including the first success, so
k \ge 1 and the mean is 1/p. The other common convention counts failures before it,
giving k \ge 0 and mean (1-p)/p. Both are called geometric; state which you are using.

Two random variables X, Y are independent iff their joint mass function (discrete) or density (continuous) factorizes:f_{X,Y}(x, y) = f_X(x)\, f_Y(y).

Both cases matter here: the sample in P-Set 0’s joint-pmf item is discrete, and the MLE examples in Chapter 2 include both.
Independence makes the likelihood of a sample factor into a product — the starting point of MLE (Ch. 2).

For any X, Y and constants a, b:\mathbb{E}[a X + b Y] = a\, \mathbb{E}[X] + b\, \mathbb{E}[Y].

This holds even when X and Y are dependent — a frequent source of slick arguments.

\mathrm{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2 \mathrm{Var}(X) + b^2 \mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2ab\, \mathrm{Cov}(X, Y).

For IID samples (so \mathrm{Cov} = 0, all \mathrm{Var} = \sigma^2), the variance of the sample mean is\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n},

giving the famous 1/\sqrt{n} shrinkage of the standard error. This is the workhorse fact behind both Monte Carlo error analysis (Ch. 3) and the \sqrt{t} scaling of random walks (Ch. 5).

For IID X_i with finite mean \mu:\bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \xrightarrow[n \to \infty]{} \mu.

“Sample averages converge to expectations.” Justifies estimating expectations by simulation.

For IID X_i with mean \mu and finite variance \sigma^2:\sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mu) \xrightarrow[n \to \infty]{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).

“Sample means are approximately Gaussian, with width \sigma/\sqrt{n}.” Underwrites confidence intervals, the diffusion limit of random walks (Ch. 5), and the lognormal model of stock prices (Ch. 6).

CLT vs. extreme value theory. The CLT describes the bulk (sample averages). Extreme value theory (Ch. 8) describes the tail — the maximum or minimum of n samples. They have different limiting distributions and very different scaling.

If Y = g(X) with g smooth and monotone, the density of Y isf_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\, \left|\frac{d g^{-1}}{dy}\right|.

Used to derive the lognormal density (Ch. 6) from a Gaussian via Y = e^X.
Throughout, \log = \ln (natural log). The base only matters when reporting nats vs. bits; for optimization, derivatives, etc., it is a multiplicative constant that does not change the argmax.

records.content:
Groups of three, or two. Each student picks a different phenomenon, so between you the group
covers all three. All three came from what this class submitted on Exercise 0.

A graduating senior sends nearly the same résumé to a long list of postings. A few employers
reply with an invitation to a first-round interview, most send a rejection, and some never
answer. People count different things when they describe how it went: replies, interviews, or
offers. Callback rates vary by field and by year, and two people applying to the same jobs can
see very different results. University career offices publish callback and placement rates from
their own surveys, and some job platforms collect application outcomes too. Advice about how
many applications to send circulates as round numbers, and some applicants report sending
several hundred without a single interview.

A stock index finishes each trading day above, below, or level with its previous close. Across
long stretches of U.S. market history, up days have been somewhat more common than down days.
Newsletter writers, fund managers and anonymous accounts publish calls on the market’s
direction, over horizons that run from the next close to the next year. Some of them have long
runs of correct calls behind them, and those runs are what the marketing quotes. Daily closing
prices for the major indexes are free and go back decades, so a call written down in advance
can be checked later against what happened.

A supply contract states limits for a part, and it may also require that at least 99% of parts
fall inside them. Lines drift as tools wear and materials change. Inspecting every part is
often impractical, so a company checks a sample from each batch and decides on that basis
whether to accept the batch, hold it, or send it back. Both errors are expensive: rejecting a
good batch holds up production, and accepting a bad one ships defects to a customer. A line
that is meeting its target will still
produce the occasional sample that looks bad, and a line that has started to drift will still
produce samples that look fine. How many parts get inspected, and what result triggers a
rejection, are set by the contract, by industry standards, and by what the defects would cost.

Frame it as a modelling problem to your agent, in a prompt of your own. You can leave it open
and see what the agent does with it. You can also try constraining it, by making explicit
assumptions or by focusing on the particular aspects of the phenomenon that interest you.
Either is a reasonable thing to do.

Whatever else you ask for, ask for these:

an explanation of its approach, and a justification for it;

its assumptions, made explicit rather than left in the code;

artifacts: markdown documents, runnable code, etc.
